name: Śrī Yantra
description: The Śrī Yantra as 11 equations in 16 unknowns, scrambled and solved again with Newton's method.
aria: The Sri Yantra drawn in light, with its triple intersection points solved live
intro: Nine triangles must interlock so that three lines cross at a single point, eleven times over. That is very hard to draw by hand. Here it becomes a system of equations solved in front of you.
legend: swelling rose dot: they miss (size = error)

tutorial.b: Four triangles point up and five point down.
In 11 places three lines must cross at exactly one point. Green dots mark them.
Scramble moves every triangle. The dots turn red and grow to show how far off they are.
Newton's method fixes all 11 points together. The graph in the corner shows the error dropping fast.
This changes one free height and solves again. The new yantra is still exact.

sound:
The pitch is the precision. Each Newton step plucks a note that rises with how many digits of the solution are exact (−log₁₀ of the error). While solving, the notes climb fast, which is the quadratic convergence you can see in the graph.

The bowl rings when all eleven triple points are exact to 10⁻¹².

Every chamber plays in Raag Bhupali: five notes, Sa Re Ga Pa Dha, tuned as whole-number ratios of the home note Sa (138.6 Hz here): 1, 9/8, 5/4, 3/2, 5/3. Simple ratios mean the sound waves line up every few cycles, so they never clash. That lets the math pick any note it likes and it still sounds like music. Underneath, a tanpura drone holds Sa and Pa, and a bansuri improvises in the same raag. The santoor and the singing bowl are the ones the math plays.

faq.a: A point where three lines of the yantra pass through exactly one spot. There are 11 per half, and they're what makes it hard to draw.
Write each line as Ax + By + C = 0. Three lines meet at one point exactly when the 3×3 determinant of their (A, B, C) rows is zero.

faq.q: how does newton's method work here?
faq.a: Hold the 5 free heights fixed, linearise the 11 equations with a finite-difference Jacobian, solve for a step, and halve it if the error would grow. A few steps reach 10⁻¹⁶.
16 unknowns (9 heights, 7 widths) minus 11 equations leaves 5. Fix any 5 heights and the rest of the yantra is determined.
Traditionally, the four upward triangles are Śiva and the five downward ones are Śakti. Their interlocking is the yantra's meaning.
It's one well-defined mathematical idealisation, following Kulaichev (1984). Traditional yantras vary, and Tahta (1992) questions some claims about the geometry.
Bhupali uses five notes, Sa Re Ga Pa Dha, tuned as the ratios 1, 9/8, 5/4, 3/2 and 5/3. It has no half-steps, so any note the math picks sounds consonant against the drone.

Sa is 138.6 Hz. Every other note is Sa times a whole-number ratio (9/8, 5/4, 3/2, 5/3) or that times a power of 2 for higher octaves. Which note plays is chosen by a number in the scene. Open 'why this sound' to watch it live.
The haze behind the math is a kaleidoscope shader. Its symmetry follows the chamber's math, but it's decoration. Say 'glow 0' to switch it off and see only the math.
Isha Maini, a data science student at Emory. Each chamber's math is written and tested in Python and JavaScript before it's drawn.
